text: Everything in this chapter so far — Services, Ingress, DNS — quietly assumed Pods could already reach each other, and by default they can. A stock cluster applies zero restrictions on which Pod can talk to which, in any namespace. A compromised public-facing frontend can, by default, open a connection straight to your payments database or an internal admin API. That's fine in a demo. In production it's a real liability, and this lesson is about closing it with NetworkPolicy.

A NetworkPolicy restricts ingress and egress traffic for Pods matching a label selector, the same mechanism Services already use. But it only matters if the cluster's CNI plugin actually enforces it — Calico and Cilium do, while some of the most basic CNI setups quietly ignore NetworkPolicy objects altogether. Confirming your cluster's CNI actually enforces policy is the first real step before relying on this for security.

Read this one like a firewall rule. podSelector picks who the policy protects — every Pod labeled app: payments-api. policyTypes: Ingress means it governs incoming traffic. The ingress block's from.podSelector names who's allowed in: only Pods labeled app: frontend, and only on TCP port 8080. Any other Pod, in any other namespace, can no longer reach payments-api at all once this exists — nothing about the Service itself changed.

Because policies combine rather than override each other, the standard production pattern is deny-all first, then carve out exceptions. podSelector: {} with no matchLabels selects every Pod in the billing namespace. With no ingress or egress rules listed, this blocks all incoming and outgoing traffic for every one of those Pods — the safest starting point, with specific allow-rules like the previous one added deliberately on top.

kubectl describe networkpolicy is the command to reach for when traffic that should work is getting blocked. It prints the exact pod selector, the allowed peers, and the allowed ports for that policy — usually enough to spot a label mismatch between the policy and the Pods it was actually supposed to cover.

That closes out Kubernetes networking: Services giving Pods a stable address, Ingress sharing one entry point across many of them, CoreDNS letting Pods find each other by name, and NetworkPolicy deciding who's even allowed to try. Chapter 5 moves to storage — PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, and the workloads that actually need to keep data around between restarts.
